scene.testo: On February 23, 1997, a fire burned for about fourteen minutes aboard a space station. Six people were trapped inside. One escape capsule was cut off by the flames. They all survived. Here is how cosmonauts survived their deadliest disasters.
But the fire was not the only killer. Smoke, a hole in the hull, and a runaway spacecraft all tried to finish the job. Each one nearly ended a mission. Each one taught a brutal lesson.
So how do you survive when there is no fire department, no ambulance, and no exit door? Three things kept these crews alive. You will get all three. And the last one comes with a twist.

Imagine you are floating inside a station at six in the morning. You are about 250 miles above Earth. You are moving at 17,500 miles per hour. Outside, temperatures swing between minus 250 and plus 250 degrees Fahrenheit.
Only a thin metal wall protects you. Your whole world is a few hundred cubic feet of air. Everything you breathe, drink, and keep warm is made or recycled inside one fragile shell.
Now an alarm sounds. A loud, harsh tone. Lights flash. Your heart jumps. There is nowhere to run. The only help is the crew beside you and the training stored in your head.

The Soviet Union and later Russia built the first long-term space stations. Salyut, then Mir. Cosmonauts lived on them for months at a time. And they met emergencies that no one had ever faced before.
Mir launched in 1986. It stayed in orbit for about fifteen years. It was built piece by piece, module by module, until it became a sprawling maze of cables, hatches, and equipment.
A maze is dangerous in an emergency. Cables run everywhere. Hatches are small. Visitors come and go on docked ships. On this station, a single blocked path could decide who lived and who did not.

Fire is the emergency every crew fears most. In microgravity, flames behave strangely. They do not rise. They form a rounded blob, because hot air does not climb without gravity. NASA still studies this with experiments.

Now the day itself. February 23, 1997. Mir carries six people, including three Russian crew members and one American. Visitors are aboard too. It is a busy station, and no one expects what comes next.
A canister that makes oxygen is lit. These devices produce breathable air through a chemical reaction. This time, something goes wrong. The canister erupts, and a flame shoots out like a blowtorch.
Thick smoke floods the module. Visibility drops. The crew can barely see each other. And the flame is burning near the path to one of the two Soyuz escape capsules. Half the lifeboats are cut off.
The crew puts on masks. They grab fire extinguishers. They fight the flames inside a sealed metal tube, hundreds of miles above Earth, with no way to open a window and let the smoke out.

According to accounts of the incident, the fire burned for roughly fourteen minutes. Fourteen minutes of heat, smoke, and fear. When it finally went out, the station stayed filled with smoke for hours.
Everyone survived. The crew cleaned the air and kept the mission going. But the lesson was clear. Always keep a clear path to your escape vehicle. That rule shapes station design to this day.

Here is the comparison with Earth. At home, you leave a burning building through a door. In orbit, your door is a capsule parked outside. Evacuation means a hatch, a spacecraft, and a fall through the atmosphere.

Today, every station module carries fire detectors, portable extinguishers, and breathing masks. Crews rehearse fire drills on a regular schedule. Each drill is built on lessons paid for by the people who lived through the real thing.
But smoke was not Mir's only crisis. Four months later, a far more dangerous accident struck. This time, the enemy was not fire. It was a collision. And it came from a spacecraft meant to help.
On June 25, 1997, a Russian cargo ship called Progress was being flown by hand toward Mir. The crew was testing a manual docking system. The spacecraft drifted off course. And it did not stop.

The cargo ship slammed into a module called Spektr. A solar panel was crushed. The hull was punctured. Air began rushing out of the station into the vacuum of space. A slow, silent leak, hundreds of miles up.
The crew had to act fast. Pressure was dropping. The only way to save the rest of the station was to seal the damaged module. That meant closing a hatch. And cables ran straight through it.
They cut the cables. They sealed the hatch. The leaking module was sacrificed to save the station. It is a decision no one wants to make, but in space, you cannot save everything. You save the crew.

The station survived. The crew survived. But the damage was serious, and the power supply suffered. Repairs would take months. This is the second pillar of survival: backups. Every critical system needs another way to work.
Air, power, cooling, and communications each have more than one path. On a modern station, sensors track pressure all day. Even a slow leak is measured in hours, which gives the crew time to respond.

The modern International Space Station faced its own leak. On August 30, 2018, ground teams noticed a slow drop in air pressure. The cause was a tiny hole in a docked Soyuz spacecraft. It was about two millimeters wide.

That is smaller than a pencil. Yet air was slipping out. The station holds air at about 14.7 pounds per square inch, the same as sea level. Outside is a near-perfect vacuum. A leak pushes outward every hour.
The crew was woken. The hole was found. They plugged it first with a finger, then with tape and a sealant. The pressure stabilized. A tiny hole, taken seriously, never became a big one.

Why take two millimeters so seriously? Because in space, small problems grow. A hole can widen. A crack can spread. That is why teams on the ground watch every number, around the clock, on every station system.
Mission control is not just a room of screens. It is hundreds of specialists who can test a fix on Earth before the crew tries it in space. That ground team is the first pillar of survival.

Now step outside. Imagine you are on a spacewalk, floating about 250 miles above Earth. Your suit is a personal spacecraft. It holds air, water, power, and cooling. One small mistake out here can become life-threatening.

On July 16, 2013, astronaut Luca Parmitano was on a spacewalk when water began collecting in his helmet. NASA's investigation documented it. At first, it seemed small. Then it grew and covered his eyes and nose.

He could barely see. He could barely hear. Water clung to his face because there was no gravity to pull it down. The walk was ended early, and he had to return to the airlock, blind and breathing carefully.

Crew inside pulled him in and removed his helmet. Investigators found a blockage in the suit's cooling system had sent water into the helmet. About a pint and a half had gathered, according to NASA's report.

After that near miss, NASA added a snorkel-like breathing tube and absorbent pads inside the helmet. A small change with a big purpose. Every close call becomes a new rule and a new piece of hardware.

Compare that to scuba diving. A diver can swim to the surface. An astronaut cannot. The only safe place is the airlock, sometimes hundreds of feet away along a handrail, with a tether as the only lifeline.

This brings us to the third pillar: training. Astronauts and cosmonauts spend years practicing emergencies before they fly. They rehearse fires, leaks, and rescues in simulators and in giant pools. They repeat each step until it becomes habit.

NASA's pool near Houston, the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory, holds about 6.2 million gallons of water. That is roughly nine Olympic-sized swimming pools. Full-size station mockups sit on the bottom, ready for practice.
Now imagine the final test: coming home. You strap into a Soyuz capsule, about the size of a small car interior. The engines fire, and the capsule drops from orbit toward the atmosphere.

Reentry heat reaches about 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit outside the capsule. A heat shield takes the blast. Then parachutes open, and a last burst of rockets softens the landing on the Kazakh steppe. It is a controlled crash.

Sometimes the return goes off script. In 2008, a Soyuz capsule came in on a steeper path than planned. The crew felt far higher gravity forces, and the capsule landed far from its target. Rescue teams found them, and the crew was fine.

Recovery teams are always waiting, because even a normal landing can be rough. Helicopters and trucks stand by. Medical staff check each crew member right at the capsule before anyone is allowed to walk.

Now I have to be honest. Not every emergency ends well. In 1986 and 2003, two space shuttle missions ended in tragedy, with all seven crew members lost each time. Those losses changed NASA's safety rules and culture.

Every safety rule on a station today was written because someone learned a hard lesson, sometimes at a terrible cost. Yet the record shows steady progress. Crews learn, systems improve, and the next generation flies safer.
The International Space Station has been continuously occupied since November 2, 2000. That is more than two decades of people living in orbit, solving problems as they appear, one alarm at a time.

So here are your three answers. One: a huge ground team that solves problems alongside the crew. Two: backups for nearly every critical system. Three: years of training until emergency steps become second nature.

Back on Earth, you rarely face a problem where the nearest help is 250 miles straight down. Crews in orbit do, every single day. Their safety comes from preparation, humility, and learning from every close call.

And here is the most surprising detail. That 2018 leak was only two millimeters wide, yet it was treated like a crisis. They do not survive because space is safe. They survive because they respect how dangerous it is. Subscribe to Orbital Days.

descrizione:
How do astronauts and cosmonauts survive fire, leaks, and spacewalk emergencies? From the 1997 Mir fire, where six people were trapped, to the tiny 2018 leak on the International Space Station, this is what really happens when disaster strikes in orbit.

We break down the three things that keep crews alive: a huge ground team, backup systems, and years of training. Plus Luca Parmitano's helmet incident, Soyuz landings, and the hard lessons behind every space station safety rule, based on NASA accounts and documented reports.
